lessons.title: Black America in 1954: Segregation, Voting and the NAACP

before.content_html:
Black America on the Eve of Brown

In 1954, almost ninety years after the abolition of slavery, the daily life of a Black American in the South was shaped by a system called Jim Crow. Schools, hospitals, buses, parks, water fountains and even cemeteries were marked ‘White’ or ‘Colored’. The Supreme Court’s 1896 ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson had blessed this with the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’. In practice, ‘separate’ was enforced by law and custom; ‘equal’ was a fiction. Black schools in Mississippi spent roughly a quarter of what white schools spent per pupil, and many Black children walked past well-funded white schools to reach their own.

Key Fact

By 1954, segregation in the South was both legal and customary. De jure segregation ran through state laws, while de facto segregation shaped Northern cities through housing and employment.

Voting: A Right on Paper Only

The Fifteenth Amendment had granted Black men the vote in 1870, but Southern states had spent eighty years stripping it back. By 1954, fewer than 20 per cent of eligible Black voters in the Deep South were registered. Mississippi was the worst, with under 5 per cent registered. The barriers were deliberate. Literacy tests demanded that applicants interpret obscure passages of the state constitution to a white registrar’s satisfaction; the same registrar would wave through illiterate white applicants.

Poll taxes required citizens to pay a fee — sometimes cumulative across years — before they could register. White-only primaries, ‘grandfather clauses’ (which exempted anyone whose grandfather had voted before 1867) and the threat of being fired, evicted or attacked completed the system. Registering to vote could cost a sharecropper his livelihood; voting could cost him his life.

Students often assume that segregation simply meant Black and white facilities sat side by side. The truth was sharper. In 1950 the average white teacher in South Carolina earned roughly twice what a Black teacher earned. Black hospital wards routinely lacked equipment that white wards took for granted. Buses required Black passengers to pay at the front, then re-board at the rear; if the white section filled up, Black passengers had to give up their seats and stand. The point of Jim Crow was not parallel facilities but daily reminders of inferior status.

The NAACP: Lawyers Building a Case

Founded in 1909 by W. E. B. Du Bois and others, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) was the largest civil rights body of the era. By 1954 it had around 400,000 members. Its strategy was patient and legalistic: train Black lawyers, identify the right plaintiffs, take cases through the federal courts and chip away at Plessy piece by piece. Thurgood Marshall, head of the NAACP’s Legal Defense Fund, had won a string of victories in higher education during the late 1940s before turning to the schools.

The NAACP also published The Crisis magazine, lobbied Congress for federal anti-lynching laws (which the Senate repeatedly blocked) and supported local branches investigating police brutality. White supremacists understood the threat: in many Southern states the NAACP was harassed by lawsuits and, by 1956, banned outright in Alabama. Membership records were demanded, and members lost jobs and homes for their affiliation.

CORE: Direct Action Before the Movement

A second organisation took a different approach. The CORE (Congress of Racial Equality) was founded in Chicago in 1942 by James Farmer and an interracial group of pacifists influenced by Mahatma Gandhi. CORE pioneered the sit-in long before Greensboro — Chicago restaurants integrated under CORE pressure in the 1940s. Its 1947 ‘Journey of Reconciliation’ sent integrated bus riders into the upper South and previewed the Freedom Rides of 1961.

Through the 1950s CORE remained smaller than the NAACP and concentrated in Northern cities, but its commitment to nonviolent direct action — deliberately breaking unjust laws and accepting arrest — gave the later movement a working playbook. Many famous campaigners, including Bayard Rustin who advised Martin Luther King, came from this CORE tradition.

Many students treat 1954 as the start of the civil rights story. Historians who write about the ‘long movement’ argue that the foundations were laid much earlier — by Black newspapers, the NAACP’s 1930s anti-lynching campaign, A. Philip Randolph’s 1941 March on Washington threat which forced Roosevelt to ban segregation in defence industries, and the activism of Black women like Ella Baker and Septima Clark in adult literacy and citizenship schools. The 1954 ruling did not create the movement; the movement created the conditions for the ruling.

Key Fact

Two distinct strategies were already in place by 1954. The NAACP used the courts and lobbying; CORE used nonviolent direct action. The mass-protest movement that exploded after Montgomery drew on both, but neither organisation invented civil rights activism — both inherited decades of earlier struggle.

A System Ready to Crack

By the early 1950s, several pressures were converging on Jim Crow. Black soldiers had returned from a war against Nazi racism and refused to accept segregation at home. Northern migration during the 1940s had given Black voters new political weight in cities like Detroit and Chicago. The Cold War made American segregation a propaganda gift to the Soviet Union, embarrassing successive administrations. The NAACP’s legal strategy was reaching the Supreme Court. The system that had governed Black life for half a century was about to face its first real legal test — Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka.

lessons.title: Brown v. Topeka 1954: A Legal Earthquake

before.content_html:
A Case Built Brick by Brick

In 1950 a welder called Oliver Brown tried to enrol his eight-year-old daughter Linda at the all-white Sumner Elementary School, four blocks from the family home in Topeka, Kansas. The school district refused. Linda was bussed across town to the all-Black Monroe Elementary instead. Topeka had segregated elementary schools but integrated high schools, and the buildings were not glaringly unequal — the system itself was the injury. That made it the perfect test case for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and its director, Thurgood Marshall, who was looking to overturn the doctrine of segregation itself, not just unequal funding.

The Topeka suit was bundled with four others from Delaware, South Carolina, Virginia and Washington D.C. into a single appeal known as Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka. Marshall argued before the Supreme Court that segregation, however materially equal, branded Black children as inferior and damaged their development. He drew on social-science evidence including the doll experiments of psychologists Kenneth and Mamie Clark, who had shown Black children consistently identifying white dolls as ‘nice’ and Black dolls as ‘bad’ — evidence cited in the eventual ruling.

Key Fact

The 1954 ruling overturned the 1896 case Plessy v. Ferguson, which had established the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’. Brown declared that ‘separate educational facilities are inherently unequal’.

The Ruling: 17 May 1954

Chief Justice Earl Warren, recently appointed by Eisenhower, was determined to deliver the ruling unanimously. He spent months persuading reluctant Southern justices that a 9-0 decision would land with greater authority than a split court. On 17 May 1954 he read the opinion himself: ‘Does segregation of children in public schools solely on the basis of race … deprive the children of the minority group of equal educational opportunities? We believe that it does.’ The court ruled school segregation a violation of the Fourteenth Amendment’s equal-protection clause. Sixty years of Plessy were swept aside in a single sentence.

The reaction was immediate. The Black press celebrated — the Pittsburgh Courier called it ‘the second emancipation’. President Eisenhower, by contrast, refused to endorse the ruling publicly and later told a friend that appointing Warren had been ‘the biggest damn-fool mistake I ever made’. White Southern leaders responded with what they called ‘massive resistance’. Within two years 101 Southern members of Congress had signed the Southern Manifesto denouncing the ruling and pledging to use ‘all lawful means’ to reverse it.

Brown II and ‘All Deliberate Speed’

The first Brown decision said segregation was unconstitutional. It did not say when or how desegregation should happen. A year later, on 31 May 1955, the Supreme Court issued a second ruling known as Brown II, which ordered Southern districts to desegregate ‘with all deliberate speed’ and left enforcement to local federal judges.

The phrase was a compromise — designed to win Southern justices’ support — and a disaster for desegregation. ‘Deliberate speed’ was contradictory enough to mean almost anything, and Southern districts read it as ‘take your time’. Ten years after the original ruling, fewer than 2 per cent of Black children in the eleven Southern states attended integrated schools. Virginia closed Prince Edward County’s public schools entirely from 1959 to 1964 rather than integrate, leaving Black children without education for five years.

A common mistake is to write that Brown ‘ended segregation’. It did not. The 1954 ruling created a legal opening; closing that opening took marshals, troops, repeated lawsuits and another decade of activism. Eisenhower had to federalise the Arkansas National Guard and send the 101st Airborne to Little Rock in 1957. Governor Faubus then closed all Little Rock’s high schools for 1958-59 rather than integrate. Real desegregation in many Southern districts dates from the 1964 Civil Rights Act and the 1968 Green v. New Kent County ruling, not 1954. Top-band answers separate the legal change from the lived change.

Significance Beyond the Schools

Even with massive resistance, Brown’s significance was huge. It signalled that the federal courts would no longer protect segregation. It encouraged activists to challenge other Jim Crow laws, knowing the legal terrain had shifted. It supplied a moral language — ‘separate is inherently unequal’ — that movement leaders deployed for the next decade. Rosa Parks later said the ruling gave Black Southerners hope; it was, she argued, part of the climate that made Montgomery thinkable just eighteen months later.

It also exposed the federal government’s reluctance to enforce its own constitutional commitments. Without Eisenhower behind it, Brown’s words sat on paper. Without the movement — without Emmett Till’s funeral, the Montgomery boycott, the Little Rock Nine, and Birmingham — those words might have stayed there. The ruling was a beginning. The work belonged to ordinary people.

Some historians celebrate Brown as the watershed of the civil rights era — the moment America’s highest court turned against legal racism. Others, including legal scholars who study what actually changed in Southern classrooms, argue that the ruling has been over-credited; without movement pressure and federal enforcement, integration on the ground was negligible until the 1960s. This is a productive split for interpretation answers: the same legal text can be read as a dramatic break or as words on paper depending on what evidence the historian foregrounds.

Key Fact

The combination of Brown I (1954) and Brown II (1955) declared school segregation unconstitutional but left enforcement to local courts. Ten years on, fewer than 2 per cent of Black children in the South attended integrated schools.

lessons.title: Montgomery 1955-56: The Boycott That Made King

before.description: Rosa Parks’s planned arrest, the 381-day boycott, the SCLC and the rise of Martin Luther King.
before.content_html:
Montgomery’s Buses Before December 1955

Montgomery, Alabama, ran its city buses on the standard Southern model. Black passengers paid the driver at the front of the bus, then climbed off and re-entered through the rear door. They sat from the back forward; white passengers from the front backward. When the white section filled, Black passengers were ordered to surrender their seats and stand. Many drivers were openly hostile, slamming doors as Black customers walked round to the rear. By 1955 around 75 per cent of Montgomery’s bus passengers were Black, but the drivers were entirely white.

The injustice had been documented and organised long before 1955. The Montgomery Women’s Political Council (WPC), led by Jo Ann Robinson, had been gathering complaints and drafting boycott plans since 1953. They were waiting for the right test case — a respected, unmistakably blameless Black woman whose arrest they could rally the city around. They had considered Claudette Colvin, a 15-year-old who had been arrested in March 1955 for refusing to give up her seat, but she was unmarried and pregnant, and the WPC feared opponents would use her circumstances to discredit the cause.

Rosa Parks: An Activist, Not a Tired Seamstress

Rosa Parks, secretary of the Montgomery NAACP, was forty-two years old, married, and had spent much of 1955 at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee studying nonviolent direct action. On the evening of 1 December 1955 she boarded a city bus on Cleveland Avenue, took a seat in the ‘coloured’ section behind the white section, and refused the driver’s order to give up her seat for a white passenger. She was arrested.

The popular memory of Parks — a tired seamstress acting on impulse — misses how prepared she was. She was an experienced organiser whose case the WPC was waiting to use. That night Jo Ann Robinson and three of her students mimeographed 35,000 leaflets calling for a one-day bus boycott on Monday 5 December. Parks’s arrest had finally given them the ‘right’ case.

Key Fact

The Montgomery Bus Boycott was not a spontaneous act. The Women’s Political Council had been preparing for two years and chose Rosa Parks — a respected NAACP organiser — deliberately. Tens of thousands of leaflets were distributed within 36 hours.

A New Voice: Martin Luther King Jr.

On the evening of 5 December, after a successful one-day boycott, Black community leaders met at Holt Street Baptist Church to decide what came next. They formed the Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA) and elected as its president a 26-year-old newcomer who had only arrived in Montgomery the previous year: Martin Luther King Jr. He had a doctorate from Boston University, a strong preaching voice, and crucially — as a recent arrival — few enemies in the city. King had not chosen leadership; leadership chose him. His speech that night, broadcast over loudspeakers to a crowd that overflowed the church, set the rhetorical template for the next decade. ‘There comes a time when people get tired of being trampled over by the iron feet of oppression,’ he told them.

The MIA voted to continue the boycott until three demands were met: courteous treatment by drivers, first-come first-served seating with no white-only section, and the hiring of Black drivers on Black-majority routes. The city refused. The boycott ran for 381 days.

Sustaining a 381-Day Walk

Sustaining the boycott took organisation that the heroic-leader version of the story often hides. Black women, who made up the majority of bus passengers, walked, hitched, or used a complex car-pool of around 300 vehicles dispatched from 48 pickup points. Black-owned taxi firms charged the same 10-cent bus fare; when the city banned this, the MIA bought station wagons. White employers who relied on Black domestic labour pressured city hall to settle — and were ignored. The boycott’s discipline was extraordinary: through Christmas, through winter rain, through indictments under a 1921 anti-boycott law, through the firebombing of King’s house in January 1956.

A common shorthand collapses Montgomery into ‘Rosa Parks sat down so Martin Luther King could stand up’. The reality is fuller. Jo Ann Robinson and the WPC drafted boycott plans years before December 1955. E. D. Nixon of the Pullman porters’ union and the NAACP arranged Parks’s bail and called for the protest. Tens of thousands of Black women walked to work for over a year. King provided eloquent leadership of an organisation that already existed; the boycott was sustained by ordinary participants and a deep network of Black churches, unions and women’s clubs. Top-band interpretation answers can use this to challenge a heroic-leader reading.

The Legal Win: Browder v. Gayle

The boycott’s decisive victory was not a city-hall surrender but a federal court ruling. The MIA’s lawyer Fred Gray filed Browder v. Gayle on behalf of four Black women including Claudette Colvin. On 13 November 1956 the Supreme Court affirmed a lower-court ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The order reached Montgomery on 20 December 1956. King boarded an integrated bus at 5:55 a.m. the following morning. The boycott had lasted 381 days.

From the MIA to the SCLC

Out of Montgomery came a new national vehicle for the movement. In January 1957 King and other Southern Black ministers founded the SCLC (Southern Christian Leadership Conference) in Atlanta. Built around Black churches — Southern institutions outside white financial control — the SCLC made nonviolent direct action the central strategy of King’s wing of the movement. Eisenhower also signed the Civil Rights Act 1957, the first since Reconstruction.

The 1957 Act was the first federal civil rights legislation since Reconstruction — a real symbolic break. But Lyndon Johnson, then Senate Majority Leader, had stripped it of meaningful enforcement to get past Southern Democratic opposition; Senator Strom Thurmond filibustered it for over 24 hours even so. The Act created a Civil Rights Commission and gave federal courts limited authority over voting-rights violations, but Black voter registration in Mississippi did not move — transformative federal action had to wait until 1964 and 1965. The Act’s real value was political: it put civil rights back on the federal agenda and tested the procedural levers that the 1964 and 1965 Acts would later use successfully.

Key Fact

Montgomery succeeded because Black passengers were the majority of bus customers, the MIA had the organisation to sustain a year-long boycott, and the federal courts — not local government — eventually ordered desegregation through Browder v. Gayle (1956).

lessons.title: Sit-Ins, Freedom Riders and James Meredith, 1960-62

before.content_html:
Greensboro and the Sit-In Movement, 1960

On 1 February 1960, four Black students from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College — Ezell Blair, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil and David Richmond — sat down at the ‘whites only’ lunch counter of the Woolworth’s store in Greensboro, North Carolina. They were refused service. They stayed in their seats until the store closed. The next day they returned with twenty more students. By the end of the week the protest had grown to several hundred, and within two months sit-ins had spread to fifty-five cities across thirteen states.

The Greensboro Four were not acting on impulse. They had read about Mahatma Gandhi’s nonviolent campaigns in India, watched the Montgomery Bus Boycott on television, and worked through how to behave under provocation. Sit-in students dressed neatly, brought textbooks to study at the counter, and were trained to absorb verbal abuse, lit cigarettes pushed into their hair and food poured over them without responding. Press photographs of well-dressed students sitting calmly while white teenagers screamed at them did the persuading.

Key Fact

The Greensboro sit-in began on 1 February 1960 with four Black students at a Woolworth’s lunch counter. Within two months sit-ins had spread to 55 cities across 13 states — the fastest mass mobilisation the movement had yet seen.

Ella Baker and the Founding of SNCC

In April 1960 Ella Baker, a veteran NAACP and SCLC organiser, convened a conference of 200 student sit-in leaders at Shaw University in Raleigh, North Carolina. Baker had spent decades organising for the NAACP and was suspicious of what she called the ‘messianic’ leadership style of Martin Luther King and the SCLC. She urged the students to set up their own independent organisation rather than become a youth wing of the SCLC. They followed her advice and founded the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC, pronounced ‘snick’).

SNCC’s commitment to participatory, bottom-up leadership, with decisions taken collectively rather than by a single charismatic figure, shaped the movement throughout the 1960s. Where the SCLC ran set-piece campaigns around King, SNCC sent organisers to live in Black communities in the rural Deep South, registering voters and running freedom schools.

The Freedom Riders, 1961

In 1960 the Supreme Court ruling in Boynton v. Virginia had extended desegregation to interstate bus terminals — waiting rooms, lunch counters and toilets used by passengers crossing state lines. Across the South the ruling was simply ignored. In May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) launched the Freedom Riders to test it. Thirteen activists, seven Black and six white, set out from Washington DC on two buses bound for New Orleans. Black riders would use the white waiting rooms and white riders the Black ones, daring local police to arrest them in violation of federal law.

The first ten days were relatively quiet. Then on 14 May 1961 the buses reached Alabama. Outside Anniston, a Ku Klux Klan mob slashed the tyres of one bus, forced it to stop, and firebombed it. Photographs of the burning Greyhound, with its passengers staggering away through smoke, ran on front pages around the world. The other bus was attacked when it reached Birmingham; the local police commissioner Bull Connor had given the Klan fifteen minutes’ head start before sending officers. The Klan beat riders unconscious with iron bars at the bus station.

The original CORE riders were too injured to continue, but a second wave of SNCC volunteers from Nashville flew to Birmingham to take their place. Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, who had wanted the rides called off to avoid embarrassing his brother before a Vienna summit with Khrushchev, found himself forced to send 600 federal marshals to escort the buses through Alabama. When state troopers withdrew at the Mississippi border, riders were arrested in Jackson and sent to the notorious Parchman penitentiary. Over the summer of 1961 more than 400 Freedom Riders were arrested. In November the Interstate Commerce Commission, under Kennedy administration pressure, finally enforced desegregation in interstate travel. The Freedom Riders had used violence inflicted on them — broadcast on television — to force federal action in a way the sit-ins alone had not.

James Meredith and Ole Miss, 1962

The third major confrontation of these years was over higher education. James Meredith, a 29-year-old Air Force veteran, applied to the University of Mississippi (‘Ole Miss’) in 1961. The university, citing Brown v. Topeka in reverse, refused on the obvious but unstated ground that he was Black. Meredith took the university to court. In September 1962 a federal court ordered Ole Miss to admit him. Mississippi Governor Ross Barnett went on television to declare he would never permit integration; he physically blocked Meredith from registering on three separate occasions.

On the night of 30 September 1962, after Meredith had been escorted onto campus by federal marshals, a mob of 2,500 white rioters attacked the marshals with bricks, bottles and gunfire. Two people were killed (a French journalist and a local jukebox repairman) and 300 injured. President Kennedy federalised the Mississippi National Guard and ordered in 30,000 US Army troops — the largest peacetime deployment of federal troops since Reconstruction. Meredith registered the next morning. He attended classes for a year under permanent armed escort and graduated in August 1963.

All three campaigns of 1960-62 used a Supreme Court ruling that the Southern states were ignoring (Brown 1954, Boynton 1960) and forced the federal government to enforce it. What was new was the move beyond Montgomery’s economic-pressure model to deliberate, planned confrontation. Activists chose the segregated lunch counter, the interstate bus, the segregated university, knowing each would generate violence and that television cameras would broadcast that violence into Northern living rooms. The strategy reframed civil rights from a Southern problem to a national one, and pulled the Kennedy administration — cautious about alienating Southern Democrats — into reluctant federal action.

Key Fact

Greensboro sit-ins (1960) spread to 55 cities and led to the founding of SNCC. The Freedom Riders (1961) forced the Interstate Commerce Commission to desegregate interstate travel. The Meredith case (1962) saw 30,000 federal troops deployed to integrate Ole Miss.

lessons.title: Birmingham, Washington and the Civil Rights Act, 1963-64

before.content_html:
Why Birmingham, 1963

By spring 1963 the SCLC had concluded that the slow, court-by-court progress of the Kennedy administration would never produce a federal civil rights law. Martin Luther King and his lieutenant Wyatt Tee Walker chose Birmingham, Alabama, as the campaign target precisely because they expected its police commissioner Bull Connor to react with public violence. Birmingham, nicknamed ‘Bombingham’ for the dozens of unsolved bombings of Black homes and churches since 1945, was the most rigidly segregated large city in the South. The campaign would force the country to look at what segregation actually was.

The protest began in April 1963 with sit-ins, marches and a boycott of downtown stores. King was arrested on 12 April for marching without a permit. From his cell he wrote the famous Letter from Birmingham Jail, replying to eight white moderate clergymen who had urged patience. ‘For years now I have heard the word “Wait!”’ he wrote. ‘This “Wait” has almost always meant “Never”.’ The letter became one of the founding documents of the modern civil rights canon.

The Children’s Crusade and the Fire Hoses

Adult arrests had nearly emptied the Birmingham movement’s reserves. On 2 May 1963, James Bevel of the SCLC sent over a thousand schoolchildren onto the streets in what became known as the Children’s Crusade. By the end of the day around 600 had been arrested, the youngest aged six. The next day Bull Connor ordered Birmingham police to turn high-pressure fire hoses, set strong enough to strip bark from trees, on schoolchildren, and to set police dogs on protestors. The photographs — a teenage boy in a cardigan being lunged at by a German Shepherd, children rolled along the pavement by water jets — ran on every front page in the world.

Key Fact

On 2-3 May 1963, around 1,000 Birmingham schoolchildren were arrested and others were attacked with fire hoses and police dogs on Bull Connor’s orders. Television images of the assault forced President Kennedy onto national television within days to call for federal civil rights legislation.

President Kennedy, who had moved cautiously on civil rights through 1961-62, said the photographs made him ‘sick’. On 11 June 1963 he gave a televised address to the nation in which he framed civil rights as ‘a moral issue … as old as the scriptures and as clear as the American Constitution’, and announced he would send a federal civil rights bill to Congress. He had been pushed there by Birmingham. Hours after the speech, the NAACP’s Mississippi field secretary Medgar Evers was shot dead in his driveway in Jackson.

The March on Washington, 28 August 1963

To pressure Congress to pass the bill, the major civil rights organisations agreed to hold the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. On 28 August 1963 around 250,000 people, roughly 60 per cent of them Black, gathered between the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial. It was the largest political demonstration in American history to that point. King delivered the closing speech. The prepared text laid out specific legislative demands; the closing ‘I Have a Dream’ section was largely improvised after gospel singer Mahalia Jackson called from behind him ‘Tell them about the dream, Martin’.

Popular memory reduces the March on Washington to King’s seventeen-minute speech. The day’s organisation belongs to A. Philip Randolph, the veteran Black trade unionist who had threatened a march on Washington in 1941 to force wartime fair-employment laws, and to Bayard Rustin, the gay socialist Quaker organiser who built the logistical operation of 250,000 marchers, 2,000 buses and 21 chartered trains in eight weeks. SNCC chairman John Lewis’s prepared speech, which had threatened to march ‘through the South like Sherman’, was toned down at the request of Catholic church leaders to keep the march’s ecumenical coalition intact. The day belonged to a movement, not a man.

From Kennedy to Johnson: Passing the Bill

Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas on 22 November 1963. His successor Lyndon B. Johnson, a Texan who had spent twenty years in the Senate, used Kennedy’s death as moral leverage. Five days after the assassination he told Congress that ‘no memorial oration or eulogy could more eloquently honour President Kennedy’s memory than the earliest possible passage of the civil rights bill’. Through the spring of 1964 he applied the legislative skill that had earned him the nickname ‘Master of the Senate’, twisting Republican arms to overcome a 60-day Southern Democratic filibuster — the longest in Senate history. The Civil Rights Act 1964, signed on 2 July 1964, banned segregation in public accommodations, federally funded programmes and employment, and gave the federal government real enforcement power for the first time since Reconstruction.

Freedom Summer and the Mississippi Murders

The Civil Rights Act did not address voting. In Mississippi only 6.7 per cent of eligible Black adults were registered to vote. In June 1964 SNCC, CORE and the NAACP launched Freedom Summer, sending hundreds of mainly white Northern students to register Black voters and run freedom schools. The choice of white volunteers was deliberate: organisers knew that violence against Black activists alone had been ignored, but violence against white students would generate national news.

On 21 June 1964, the project’s third day, three volunteers — James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner — disappeared near Philadelphia, Mississippi. Six weeks later, after a search involving 200 FBI agents and US Navy divers (who in the process found the bodies of eight other murdered Black men whose disappearances had never been investigated), the three were found buried in an earthen dam. They had been beaten and shot by a mob of Klansmen led by the Neshoba County deputy sheriff. The murders made the front pages and the network news exactly as the organisers had reluctantly anticipated.

Federal civil rights charges against eighteen suspects in 1967 produced seven convictions for conspiracy — not murder, since Mississippi refused to prosecute. Edgar Ray Killen, organiser of the killings, was finally convicted of manslaughter only in 2005, on the 41st anniversary of the murders. Yet Freedom Summer succeeded in two ways. It put the absence of Black voting rights at the centre of national news in summer 1964. And it produced the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, whose challenge at the 1964 Democratic Convention — led by Fannie Lou Hamer’s televised testimony of being beaten in a Mississippi jail for trying to register to vote — embarrassed Johnson and prepared the political ground for the 1965 Voting Rights Act.

Key Fact

The 1964 Civil Rights Act outlawed segregation in public accommodations, federally funded programmes and employment. It was proposed by Kennedy after the Birmingham campaign in June 1963 and passed by Lyndon Johnson on 2 July 1964 after the longest filibuster in Senate history.

The Vote: The Unfinished Business of 1964

The 1964 Civil Rights Act had banned segregation in public accommodations, schools and federally funded programmes. It had not addressed voting. Across the Deep South, Black Americans were kept off the electoral roll by a network of devices that had grown up since the end of Reconstruction in the 1870s: literacy tests set arbitrarily by white registrars, poll taxes, the requirement to bring a registered voter to vouch for the applicant, and the threat of being sacked, evicted or beaten if you tried to register. In Selma, Alabama, county seat of Dallas County, only 2 per cent of voting-age Black adults were on the register in 1965, despite Black people being a majority of the population.

Key Fact

In 1965 only 2 per cent of voting-age Black adults in Dallas County, Alabama were registered to vote, even though Black Americans were the majority of the county’s population. Across Mississippi the figure was 6.7 per cent. The 1964 Civil Rights Act had not addressed voting.

Why Selma?

SNCC organisers had been working in Selma since 1963 to register voters and to organise local people who had borne reprisals for trying. In January 1965 the SCLC, fresh from a difficult campaign in St Augustine, Florida, agreed to come to Selma at the invitation of the local Dallas County Voters League. Martin Luther King chose Selma for the same reason he had chosen Birmingham: he expected the local sheriff, Jim Clark, to react with public violence. Clark’s deputies wore lapel pins reading ‘Never’.

The campaign opened with mass attempts to register that ran straight into Clark’s tactics — long queues kept standing for hours in the rain, arrests for ‘loitering’ on courthouse steps. By the end of January 1965, 2,000 Black activists had been arrested, including King himself. On 18 February 1965, in nearby Marion, state troopers shot a 26-year-old church deacon called Jimmie Lee Jackson while he was trying to protect his mother and grandfather from a beating. Jackson died eight days later. Out of grief and anger, the SCLC announced a march from Selma to the state capital Montgomery to deliver a petition to Governor George Wallace.

Bloody Sunday, 7 March 1965

On the afternoon of Sunday 7 March 1965, around 600 marchers set out from Brown Chapel in Selma. They were led by SNCC chairman John Lewis and SCLC organiser Hosea Williams. They walked in pairs along the pavement of US Route 80, crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge over the Alabama River, and stopped where the road descended on the far side. A line of around 200 state troopers and Sheriff Clark’s mounted posse blocked the road. The troopers gave them two minutes to disperse. After ninety seconds the troopers attacked.

The marchers were charged with horses, beaten with billy clubs wrapped in barbed wire, and tear-gassed. John Lewis’s skull was fractured. Around 60 marchers were hospitalised. ABC News interrupted its scheduled film — Judgment at Nuremberg, a drama about the Nazi war-crimes trials — to broadcast 15 minutes of footage from the bridge. Forty-eight million Americans watched. Telegrams of protest poured into the White House through Sunday night. The day became known as Bloody Sunday.

King had not been on the bridge on Bloody Sunday. On Tuesday 9 March he led a second ‘turnaround’ march to the bridge, knelt, prayed and turned back to honour a federal restraining order. That night three white Unitarian ministers who had come south for the march were attacked in a Selma street; one, James Reeb, died of his injuries. Reeb’s death generated headlines and presidential condolences that Jimmie Lee Jackson’s had not — a fact King later spoke about with characteristic honesty. Federal District Judge Frank Johnson lifted the restraining order, and on 21 March a third march, this time legally protected by 2,000 federalised Alabama National Guard and 1,800 US Army troops, set off from Selma. By the time the marchers reached the Alabama State Capitol on 25 March they were 25,000 strong. King addressed them: ‘How long? Not long, because the arc of the moral universe is long but it bends toward justice.’

President Johnson’s ‘We Shall Overcome’ Speech

On 15 March 1965, eight days after Bloody Sunday, President Johnson addressed a joint session of Congress and a national television audience. He announced he was sending Congress a federal voting rights bill, and named the cause as a moral one in language no white president had used before: ‘Their cause must be our cause too. Because it is not just Negroes, but really it is all of us, who must overcome the crippling legacy of bigotry and injustice. And we shall overcome.’ The borrowing of the movement’s anthem from the lips of a Texan president was, for many in the SNCC and SCLC offices watching, the moment they realised the bill would pass.

The Voting Rights Act 1965

The Voting Rights Act 1965 was signed by Johnson in the Capitol Rotunda on 6 August 1965. It suspended literacy tests in any county where less than 50 per cent of voting-age adults had registered or voted in 1964. It authorised federal registrars to enrol voters directly in those counties — bypassing obstructive local registrars entirely. And under Section 5 it required state and local jurisdictions with a history of voting discrimination to submit any change to voting rules to the US Department of Justice for pre-clearance, to prevent the cycle of new exclusions replacing the old. The 24th Amendment of January 1964 had already abolished the federal poll tax; the 1966 Supreme Court ruling in Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections banned the state poll tax that remained.

In Mississippi, Black voter registration jumped from 6.7 per cent in 1964 to 59.8 per cent in 1968. Across the Deep South more than a quarter of a million Black voters were added to the rolls within five months of the Act being signed. Federal registrars enrolled half of them. The Act was the most effective single piece of civil rights legislation of the twentieth century. But the franchise alone did not address Northern de facto segregation, housing, policing, jobs, schools or wealth. The Watts riot in Los Angeles broke out five days after Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act, killing 34 and signalling that civil rights legislation had not addressed the urban North. The movement’s next phase, and its splintering, would be over those questions.

Key Fact

The 1965 Voting Rights Act suspended literacy tests, sent federal registrars into counties with histories of discrimination, and required Justice Department pre-clearance of changes to voting rules. By 1968, Black voter registration in Mississippi had risen from 6.7 per cent to 59.8 per cent.

lessons.title: Malcolm X and the Black Muslims, 1952-65

before.content_html:
From Malcolm Little to Malcolm X

Malcolm Little was born in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1925. His father Earl, a Baptist minister and follower of the Black-nationalist leader Marcus Garvey, was killed in 1931 in what the white-owned local press recorded as a streetcar accident and what the family always believed was a murder by white supremacists. His mother was committed to a mental hospital. Malcolm grew up in foster care, drifted into petty crime in Boston and Harlem, and in 1946, aged 20, was sentenced to ten years in prison for burglary.

In prison he encountered the Nation of Islam, a Black Muslim religious movement led by Elijah Muhammad. The Nation taught that white people were the ‘blue-eyed devils’ created by an evil scientist 6,000 years ago, that Black people were the original humans, and that integration was a trap. The doctrine made sense of everything that had happened to Malcolm’s family. He converted, took the surname ‘X’ to mark the lost African name slavery had stolen, and on his release in 1952 became a Nation minister. By the late 1950s he was the Nation’s national spokesman and Elijah Muhammad’s designated successor.

Key Fact

Malcolm Little adopted the name Malcolm X in prison after converting to the Nation of Islam in the late 1940s. The ‘X’ marked the African family name lost under slavery. By 1959 he was the Nation’s national spokesman and the public face of Black Muslim teaching in the United States.

Beliefs and Methods, 1952-63

Malcolm X’s public message in his Nation years rejected almost every assumption of King and the SCLC. Where King wanted integration, the Nation taught racial separatism and the eventual return of Black Americans to a state of their own. Where King preached nonviolent direct action, Malcolm called for self-defence ‘by any means necessary’: ‘If someone puts a hand on you, send him to the cemetery.’ Where King appealed to the conscience of white America, Malcolm dismissed that conscience as a fiction and refused to be addressed as ‘Negro’. He attacked the 1963 March on Washington as ‘the Farce on Washington’, a movement coopted by white liberal money and presidential approval.

For young Black Northerners outside the SCLC’s Southern church base — in Harlem, in Chicago, in Detroit — Malcolm articulated an anger at white America that nonviolent direct action could not contain. The Nation also offered a programme: drug rehabilitation, family discipline, Black-owned businesses, mosques, schools and newspapers funded entirely from Black donations. By 1959 the Nation had grown from around 400 members in 1952 to perhaps 50,000.

A common shorthand sets Malcolm and King up as opposites — nonviolence vs violence, integration vs separatism — and ends the story there. The reality is messier. King’s public position on self-defence inside the home was less absolute than his public sermons (he kept armed guards at his Montgomery house in 1956 and applied for a concealed-carry permit; it was refused). Malcolm’s position changed dramatically after 1964. The two men met in person only once, briefly, at the Capitol on 26 March 1964 over the Civil Rights Bill; King later wrote that Malcolm ‘had the great ability to put his finger on the existence and root of the problem’. Top-band interpretation answers can use the convergence after the Hajj to challenge a static-opposites reading.

The Break with the Nation of Islam, 1963-64

The split had two layers. In December 1963, after President Kennedy’s assassination, Malcolm called the killing ‘chickens coming home to roost’ — that is, the violence the United States visited on others, returning to it. Elijah Muhammad suspended him for ninety days. Below the surface, Malcolm had also discovered that Elijah Muhammad — who taught strict sexual discipline — had fathered children with several Nation secretaries. By March 1964 Malcolm had left the Nation entirely.

In April 1964 he flew to Saudi Arabia to perform the Hajj, the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca. Sunni Islam, with believers of every colour praying side by side, contradicted the Nation’s race theology. He wrote home from Mecca that he had seen ‘the brotherhood practiced by people of all colors’ and that he was now obliged to drop ‘sweeping indictments of one race’. He returned with the new name el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz and a public position that white people could be allies, although racism in the United States remained the system that had to be dismantled.

The Final Year and the Assassination

In June 1964 Malcolm founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity (OAAU). Modelled on the Organization of African Unity formed by newly independent African states, the OAAU aimed to take Black American grievances to the United Nations as a human rights issue. Malcolm travelled in Africa for much of 1964, met heads of state, addressed the Cairo Conference of the OAU, and began building international links unimaginable in his Nation period. SNCC organisers including Fannie Lou Hamer met him in Harlem; he travelled to Selma in February 1965 in support of the SCLC’s voting rights campaign.

The Nation, which now treated him as a heretic, had been issuing thinly veiled death threats since the spring of 1964. Malcolm’s home was firebombed on 14 February 1965; he, his wife Betty Shabazz and their four daughters escaped. Seven days later, on 21 February 1965, Malcolm took the stage at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem to address the OAAU. As he greeted the audience, three Nation of Islam members rushed the stage and shot him at close range. He was 39.

At his death, Malcolm was widely treated by the white press as a defeated demagogue. His Autobiography, published a few months later in collaboration with Alex Haley, became one of the most-read books in twentieth-century America and shaped the politics of a younger generation of activists. By 1966 SNCC had moved away from nonviolence under Stokely Carmichael, who acknowledged Malcolm as the founding voice of Black Power. Huey Newton and Bobby Seale founded the Black Panther Party in October 1966 explicitly in his memory, picking up his demand for armed Black self-defence. Malcolm’s Nation period and his Sunni-Muslim, internationalist OAAU period had to be told together to make any sense of the late-1960s movement.

Key Fact

Between December 1963 and February 1965 Malcolm X broke with the Nation of Islam, performed the Hajj as a Sunni Muslim, took the name el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz, founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity, and shifted from racial separatism to a position that white allies were possible — though American racism remained the system to be dismantled. He was assassinated by Nation members on 21 February 1965.

lessons.title: Black Power, the Panthers and the 1968 Olympics

before.content_html:
From SNCC to ‘Black Power’, 1966

By 1966 the patience that had carried the early civil rights movement was running thin among younger Black activists. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 had ended legal segregation in the South, but they had not touched ghetto poverty in Northern cities, racist policing, or de facto school and housing segregation. SNCC organisers who had been beaten on the Freedom Rides, jailed during Freedom Summer and gassed at Selma had concluded that nonviolent direct action could not, on its own, deliver Black freedom. The new mood needed a name; it was given one in Mississippi.

In June 1966 James Meredith, the air force veteran who had integrated the University of Mississippi in 1962, set out alone on a 220-mile ‘March Against Fear’ from Memphis, Tennessee to Jackson, Mississippi. On the second day a sniper shot him with birdshot. As Meredith recovered in hospital, the SCLC, CORE and SNCC took up the march together. On the evening of 16 June, after another mass arrest, the new SNCC chairman Stokely Carmichael climbed onto a truck in Greenwood and led the crowd in a call-and-response: ‘What do we want?’ — ‘Black Power!’ The phrase travelled through television and the next day’s newspapers across the country.

Key Fact

The slogan ‘Black Power’ was popularised by Stokely Carmichael, SNCC’s new chairman, on the Meredith March Against Fear in Mississippi in June 1966. It signalled SNCC’s break with the SCLC’s strategy of nonviolent integrationism and called instead for Black self-determination, separate community institutions and the right of self-defence.

What Black Power meant

Black Power was a programme as well as a chant. Carmichael argued that integration as defined by the SCLC asked Black Americans to abandon their own communities to enter white ones on white terms. He demanded political power in places where Black voters were the majority, Black control of schools and housing in Black neighbourhoods, an unembarrassed pride in African heritage, and self-defence against racist violence. The slogan ‘Black is Beautiful’, the rise of Afro hairstyles, the wearing of African clothing and the renaming of academic disciplines as ‘Black Studies’ all flowed from the same source. King distanced himself from the slogan as politically counterproductive but agreed with much of its diagnosis of Northern poverty and ghetto policing.

The Black Panther Party for Self-Defense

In Oakland, California, in October 1966, two community-college students, Huey Newton and Bobby Seale, founded the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense. Their Ten-Point Programme demanded full employment, decent housing, an end to police brutality, the release of Black prisoners and reparations for slavery. Their first public action was an armed police-monitoring patrol: Panthers in black leather jackets and berets followed Oakland police cars at a legal distance, openly carrying loaded shotguns (which California law then permitted) and citing arrestees their constitutional rights. In May 1967 thirty Panthers walked into the California state Capitol carrying rifles to protest a bill banning open carry; the protest produced national television images and a thousand new applications to join.

The Panthers also ran what they called ‘survival programmes’: a Free Breakfast for Children programme that by 1969 was feeding around 20,000 children in 19 cities every weekday morning, free health clinics, sickle-cell anaemia testing, free legal aid, escort services for the elderly to collect pensions, and Liberation Schools. By 1970 the FBI’s director J. Edgar Hoover had described the Panthers as ‘the greatest threat to the internal security of the country’ and was running them as a top target of COINTELPRO, the Bureau’s counter-intelligence programme.

Students often picture the Panthers solely through the iconic photographs of leather jackets, berets and rifles, and conclude they were a violent gang the FBI was right to crush. The historical picture is more complicated. The Panthers were targets of COINTELPRO sabotage, including forged letters that fed feuds with rival groups, paid informants inside the leadership, and police raids: on 4 December 1969 the Chicago police, working from FBI intelligence, killed the 21-year-old Illinois Panther chairman Fred Hampton in his bed during a pre-dawn raid. Top-band interpretation answers can hold the survival programmes, the armed self-defence, the criminality of some chapter members and the federal repression in the same frame, rather than picking one and discarding the rest.

The Mexico Olympics, 16 October 1968

Twelve days after Mexico City police killed an unknown number of student protesters in the Tlatelolco massacre, two Black American sprinters stood on the medal rostrum at the Mexico Olympics. Tommie Smith had won the 200m gold medal in a world record of 19.83 seconds. John Carlos had taken bronze. As The Star-Spangled Banner began, both men bowed their heads and raised a black-gloved fist in what they called a ‘human-rights salute’. They wore no shoes, in protest at Black poverty; Smith’s scarf and Carlos’s beads remembered Black Americans who had been lynched. The Australian silver medallist Peter Norman wore the same Olympic Project for Human Rights badge as the two Americans in solidarity. Within forty-eight hours the International Olympic Committee, under pressure from its president Avery Brundage, expelled Smith and Carlos from the Olympic village; both received death threats on returning home and were unable to find work for years.

For the international press the Mexico salute became the visual shorthand for Black Power. It rebuked the United States in front of a global television audience, refused to perform patriotism while Black Americans were dying in Vietnam at disproportionate rates, and stood in solidarity with the wider 1968 protest year — Paris, Prague, the Tlatelolco students, the assassinations of King in April and Robert Kennedy in June.

Key Fact

On 16 October 1968 Tommie Smith (gold) and John Carlos (bronze) raised black-gloved fists on the 200m medal rostrum at the Mexico Olympics during the US national anthem. The shoeless feet referred to Black poverty, the scarf and beads to lynching victims; both men were expelled from the Olympic village within forty-eight hours and went home to death threats and a job blacklist.

Historians who emphasise the achievements of Black Power point to the Free Breakfast programme (the Nixon administration enlarged the federal school-breakfast programme partly to outflank the Panthers); to Carmichael’s articulation of ‘institutional racism’ that has remained the standard analytical category in policy and academic writing; to the cultural break-through of Afro-American Studies, ‘Black is Beautiful’ and the Olympic salute; and to the survival programmes’ demonstration that Black communities could organise their own welfare state from below. Historians who emphasise decline point to the Panthers’ collapse under COINTELPRO surveillance, internal feuds and criminal entanglements by the mid-1970s; to the Olympic Project for Human Rights’ failure to deliver lasting institutional change inside US athletics; and to the slogan’s political cost in alienating white liberal allies that the legislative coalitions of 1964-65 had depended on. Both readings rest on solid evidence and answer Q3(d) prompts well.

lessons.title: Riots, Kerner and King's Last Year, 1965-68

before.content_html:
Why Northern Cities Burned, 1965-67

Five days after President Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act, the largest Black neighbourhood in Los Angeles erupted. On 11 August 1965 a white California Highway Patrol officer pulled over a Black driver, Marquette Frye, in Watts, a Black district of South Los Angeles. A scuffle escalated into six days of rioting that left 34 people dead, more than 1,000 injured, around 4,000 arrests and roughly $40 million of property damage. National Guard tanks rolled through Black neighbourhoods. Watts was not an isolated event. Over the next two summers a wave of urban uprisings struck cities across the North and Midwest. In July 1967 alone there were over 150 incidents; the worst were in Newark, New Jersey, where 26 people died, and in Detroit, where a five-day uprising killed 43 people. Johnson sent in 4,700 paratroopers and 8,000 National Guard.

The riots had long-term causes. Northern Black Americans had moved up from the Southern fields during the Great Migration to work in industrial cities; by 1965 those cities were losing manufacturing jobs as factories moved to the suburbs that Black families had been excluded from by ‘redlining’ (the federal practice of refusing mortgages in Black neighbourhoods). Schools were segregated by housing. Police forces were almost entirely white and routinely violent. The 1964 Civil Rights Act and 1965 Voting Rights Act had targeted the legal segregation of the South; they had not touched any of these Northern conditions.

Key Fact

Between 1965 and 1967 over 150 American cities saw urban uprisings. The biggest were Watts (Los Angeles, August 1965, 34 dead), Newark (New Jersey, July 1967, 26 dead), and Detroit (Michigan, July 1967, 43 dead). The riots showed that the legislative victories of 1964-65 had not addressed Northern poverty, housing segregation or racist policing.

The Kerner Report, February 1968

In July 1967, with Detroit still smouldering, Johnson appointed the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders, chaired by Illinois governor Otto Kerner. Johnson hoped the Kerner Report would blame outside agitators. It did the opposite. Published on 29 February 1968 the report identified white racism, segregated housing, unequal schools, mass unemployment and police behaviour as the underlying causes. It found evidence of ‘strong racist attitudes’ in around three-quarters of police departments and warned that the United States was ‘moving toward two societies, one black, one white — separate and unequal’. The Commission recommended large-scale federal investment in housing, jobs, schools and police reform, and proposed treating racial inequality with the urgency of a national emergency.

Johnson, embarrassed by the criticism of his own ‘War on Poverty’ programme as inadequate, refused to receive the report ceremonially at the White House and never publicly endorsed its recommendations. Vietnam was now consuming the federal budget. Within weeks Johnson had announced he would not seek re-election; within four months a presidential campaign that ran on the suburbs’ reaction to the riots had elected Richard Nixon, who promised ‘law and order’ and a ‘silent majority’. The Kerner recommendations were never implemented at the scale the Commission asked for.

A common misreading treats the urban uprisings of 1965-67 as proof the civil rights movement had failed, or that Black Americans were ungrateful for the 1964-65 legislation. Kerner reached the opposite conclusion. The Commission found that the rioters were not an aimless minority but a representative cross-section of young Black men in the cities concerned; that they had been provoked by specific incidents of police violence; and that the underlying conditions — housing, schools, jobs, policing — were structural rather than individual. Top-band evaluation answers can use the Kerner findings to challenge an interpretation that the post-1965 movement ‘turned violent’ or that civil rights had been substantially achieved by 1968.

King’s Chicago Campaign and the Northern Pivot, 1966-67

King had recognised the Northern question even before Watts. In January 1966 the SCLC launched the Chicago Freedom Movement, joining local activists in a campaign against slum landlords, housing segregation and discriminatory school enrolment. King and his family rented an apartment in a West Side tenement to dramatise the housing question. On a march through the all-white suburb of Marquette Park in August 1966, white residents threw bricks; King was struck, and said afterwards he had ‘never seen, even in Mississippi or Alabama, mobs as hateful as I’ve seen here in Chicago’. The settlement Mayor Richard Daley signed was vague, unenforceable and largely ignored. Chicago made plain that nonviolent direct action could not, on its own, dismantle Northern housing segregation.

In April 1967, in a speech at Riverside Church in New York, King condemned the war in Vietnam as a ‘cruel manipulation of the poor’, costing Black soldiers’ lives at disproportionate rates and starving the War on Poverty of money. The speech cost King support among white liberals, the Johnson administration and parts of the SCLC board, who feared losing federal allies. By late 1967 King had launched the Poor People’s Campaign: a multiracial march on Washington that would camp on the Mall to demand a Federal Economic Bill of Rights, a guaranteed income, decent housing and full employment.

Memphis, 4 April 1968

In February 1968 about 1,300 Black sanitation workers in Memphis, Tennessee went on strike under the banner ‘I AM A MAN’ after two refuse collectors were crushed to death by a malfunctioning truck while sheltering from the rain in its compactor — segregation policy denied them shelter inside the depot. King flew to Memphis on 18 March to support them. On 3 April, exhausted and ill, he gave the ‘Mountaintop’ sermon at the Mason Temple: ‘I’ve been to the mountaintop… I’ve seen the Promised Land. I may not get there with you.’ The next evening, just after six o’clock on 4 April 1968, as King stood on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel, a single rifle shot from the boarding house across the street killed him. He was 39.

News of the killing triggered the largest single wave of urban uprisings in American history. In the week that followed, more than 100 cities saw rioting; 39 people were killed, around 21,000 were arrested, and federal troops occupied parts of Washington and Baltimore. Robert Kennedy, campaigning in Indianapolis on a Black side of the city, broke the news to a Black audience and asked them to honour King by going home. They did. Kennedy himself was shot dead in Los Angeles two months later.

Key Fact

Martin Luther King was assassinated on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee, on 4 April 1968, at the age of 39. He had travelled to Memphis to support striking Black sanitation workers. In the week that followed, more than 100 American cities erupted in rioting, 39 people were killed and federal troops occupied Washington and Baltimore.

By 1975 the legal architecture of segregation had gone. The Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965) and Fair Housing Act (1968 — passed in the week after King’s death) had outlawed segregation in public accommodation, employment, voting and housing. Black voter registration in the South had risen from around 23 per cent in 1964 to over 60 per cent by 1969. The number of Black elected officials nationwide had risen from about 100 in 1964 to over 3,500 by 1975. But the Kerner conditions in Northern cities — segregated housing, segregated schools by housing, mass unemployment, racist policing — had not been addressed. Median Black household income remained around 60 per cent of white household income. The poverty rate of Black Americans was almost three times that of white Americans. The legal revolution was substantially complete; the economic and Northern revolution had barely begun. Top-band evaluation answers hold both readings together rather than picking one.

lessons.title: From Diem to Tonkin: US Steps into Vietnam, 1954-64

before.content_html:
Why Vietnam, and Why 1954?

In May 1954 a French army of 13,000 men surrendered at Dien Bien Phu in northern Vietnam after a fifty-six-day siege by the Vietminh, the communist-led independence movement under Ho Chi Minh. The defeat ended sixty-four years of French colonial rule in Indochina. The peace conference that followed in Geneva produced the Geneva Accords: Vietnam was partitioned at the seventeenth parallel pending nationwide reunification elections in 1956. The communists held the north (the Democratic Republic of Vietnam under Ho Chi Minh in Hanoi); a US-backed government held the south (the Republic of Vietnam under Bao Dai in Saigon, and from 1955 under Ngo Dinh Diem).

President Eisenhower’s administration would not accept that Indochina might fall to communism. In April 1954, even before Dien Bien Phu, Eisenhower had explained the danger in a press conference using a metaphor that would shape American policy for fifteen years. ‘You have a row of dominoes set up,’ he said, ‘you knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly.’ If Vietnam fell, Laos and Cambodia would follow; then Thailand, then Burma, then potentially India and Australasia. The domino theory presented the war as a single piece of a global containment strategy.

Key Fact

The domino theory was articulated by President Eisenhower in an April 1954 press conference and shaped fifteen years of US policy in Vietnam. It predicted that if South Vietnam fell to communism, the other states of Southeast Asia — Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Burma — would topple in sequence and that communism would advance towards India and Australasia. It made South Vietnam a global, not local, problem.

Eisenhower’s Man in Saigon: Ngo Dinh Diem

Ngo Dinh Diem took power as prime minister of South Vietnam in 1954 and, after a rigged 1955 referendum, declared himself president of a republic. Diem was Catholic, French-educated, anti-communist and a member of the small Mandarin landlord class in a country roughly 80 per cent Buddhist and roughly 80 per cent peasant. Eisenhower committed the United States to keeping Diem in power. Between 1955 and 1961 around $1.6 billion in US aid flowed to Saigon.

The weaknesses of the Diem government were obvious to almost everyone except Diem himself. He refused to hold the 1956 reunification elections promised at Geneva (President Eisenhower privately conceded he would have lost them). His government was openly nepotistic: his brother Ngo Dinh Nhu ran a network of secret police, and Nhu’s wife Madame Nhu acted as the regime’s public spokeswoman. Land reform, which the Vietminh had used to win peasant support in the north, was reversed in the south — landlords who had fled were brought back and rents reimposed. Catholic refugees from the north received preferential treatment in the south, including land grants and government jobs. In 1963 the regime’s repression of Buddhist demonstrations, including the live televised self-immolation of the monk Thich Quang Duc on a Saigon street in June 1963, destroyed Diem’s remaining international standing.

Students sometimes describe Diem as a corrupt strongman whose mistakes a more competent leader could have avoided. The deeper problem was structural. The Republic of Vietnam was a state with no rural legitimacy. Most of the south’s population were tenant farmers; reversing land reform handed the Vietminh a recruitment programme. The Catholic-Mandarin character of the regime alienated the Buddhist and peasant majority. The 1960 founding of the southern Vietcong — the National Liberation Front, formed by southern communists left over from the anti-French war — gave a structure to peasant grievances that Diem could not address without giving up his class base. Top-band evaluation answers will read US escalation as forced by structural weaknesses, not just by Diem’s personal failures.

Kennedy: Strategic Hamlets and 16,000 Advisers

When John F. Kennedy entered the White House in January 1961, around 800 US military ‘advisers’ were stationed in South Vietnam. By the time of his assassination in November 1963 the figure was over 16,000. Kennedy expanded covert action, helicopter support and special forces, and signed off on a counter-insurgency project copied from British operations in Malaya: the Strategic Hamlets Programme. Vietnamese peasants were forcibly relocated into fortified hamlets ringed with barbed wire and ditches to deny the Vietcong food, shelter and recruits. Around 8 million people were moved into around 8,000 such hamlets between 1962 and 1963.

The programme was a disaster. Peasants resented being uprooted from ancestral village land, often at gunpoint. Hamlets were poorly supplied and frequently overrun; the Vietcong simply waited until the relocation was complete and then walked through the wire. By late 1963 most of the hamlets had been abandoned or had effectively become Vietcong recruiting bases. Kennedy’s strategy of fighting an Asian guerrilla war on the cheap with American advisers and a Vietnamese client army had failed.

The November 1963 Coup

By the autumn of 1963 the Kennedy administration concluded that the war could not be won with Diem in power. On 1 November 1963, Saigon generals supported by US ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge launched a coup against Diem. Diem and his brother Nhu were captured the following morning and murdered in the back of an armoured personnel carrier. Three weeks later Kennedy himself was assassinated in Dallas. The new Johnson administration inherited a South Vietnam that was now politically more unstable than it had been under Diem — nine successive juntas would govern it in the first eighteen months after the coup — and a war that the United States was visibly losing.

Key Fact

Under President Kennedy, the number of US military ‘advisers’ in South Vietnam grew from around 800 to over 16,000 between 1961 and 1963. Kennedy approved the Strategic Hamlets Programme of 1962-63, which uprooted around 8 million peasants and accelerated the Vietcong’s recruitment. On 1-2 November 1963 the Kennedy administration backed a Saigon coup that overthrew and killed President Diem.

The Gulf of Tonkin Incident, August 1964

On 2 August 1964, in international waters off the North Vietnamese coast, the destroyer USS Maddox exchanged fire with three North Vietnamese torpedo boats. The Maddox was supporting covert South Vietnamese commando raids on the North Vietnamese coast. Two days later, in heavy weather, the Maddox and the destroyer USS Turner Joy reported a second engagement. The second incident never happened. Sonar operators on the Turner Joy had picked up echoes off their own propellers; no North Vietnamese boats were ever within range. The Johnson administration, deciding the truth did not matter, presented the August 4 ‘attack’ to Congress as unprovoked aggression.

On 7 August 1964 Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution. It authorised the president ‘to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack’ against US forces and to assist any Southeast Asian state under attack. The resolution passed 416-0 in the House and 88-2 in the Senate. Without ever declaring war, Johnson now had the legal authority to fight one. Within seven months he had ordered the bombing of North Vietnam (Operation Rolling Thunder, March 1965) and committed the first US ground combat units to South Vietnam.

Top-band 12-mark causation answers will weigh several factors against each other. The Tonkin Resolution provided the legal vehicle for escalation but was itself a symptom rather than a cause: by August 1964 South Vietnam’s government had collapsed nine times in nine months, the Strategic Hamlets had failed, the Vietcong controlled most of the countryside, and the domino logic that had drawn the US into Indochina under Eisenhower made withdrawal politically impossible for Johnson in an election year. The August 4 incident was the trigger; the underlying causes were the structural weakness of South Vietnam, the failure of Kennedy-era counter-insurgency, the increasing strength of the Vietcong supplied via the Ho Chi Minh Trail, and the Cold War commitment to containment that no US president from 1954 to 1968 would walk away from.

lessons.title: Tet, My Lai and the War at Home, 1968-70

before.content_html:
The War the United States Was Told It Was Winning

By the end of 1967 General William Westmoreland was telling the American public that the Vietnam War had reached a turning point. There was, he said in a White House press conference in November, ‘light at the end of the tunnel’. The Vietcong were exhausted; the body count was rising; the South Vietnamese government was stabilising. Three months later that confidence collapsed. The events of 1968 to 1970 — the Tet Offensive, Walter Cronkite’s CBS broadcast, the My Lai Massacre and the Kent State shootings — broke the credibility of the Johnson administration, divided American society into a war camp and an anti-war camp, and brought the home front and the battlefield together as a single political problem.

The Tet Offensive

On the night of 30 January 1968, during the Vietnamese lunar new year holiday, around 84,000 Vietcong and North Vietnamese soldiers launched coordinated assaults on more than a hundred cities and military bases across South Vietnam. A Vietcong commando squad blew its way into the grounds of the US embassy in Saigon and held part of it for six hours. The ancient imperial city of Hue was overrun in the first hours and held for twenty-five days. Footage of US marines fighting house to house in Hue, and of Vietcong gunmen inside the embassy compound in Saigon, ran on every American evening news bulletin.

The Tet Offensive was, in narrow military terms, a US-South Vietnamese victory. The Vietcong took catastrophic casualties — around 40,000 dead, by some estimates — and lost almost all the urban territory they had briefly seized. The southern uprising that Hanoi had hoped to provoke did not materialise. Westmoreland told a press conference in early February that he had ‘defeated the enemy’s will to win’. The political reality was the reverse. Tet contradicted the ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ assurances of November 1967 so completely that no one in the United States believed the war was being won. The gap between official optimism and televised reality produced what journalists called the credibility gap.

Key Fact

The Tet Offensive began on 30 January 1968 with coordinated Vietcong attacks on more than a hundred targets across South Vietnam. Tactically the US and South Vietnamese drove the attackers back, killing around 40,000 Vietcong and recovering Hue after twenty-five days of urban fighting. Strategically Tet shattered the Johnson administration’s ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ line, opened the credibility gap, and turned American public opinion against the war.

A common student error is to label Tet 1968 as the moment the United States ‘lost’ Vietnam militarily. Tactically Tet was a US-South Vietnamese victory: the Vietcong lost almost all the urban territory they had briefly seized, took around 40,000 casualties and were so depleted they would never again play the leading role in the war. The strategic shock was political and televisual. The offensive contradicted Westmoreland’s November 1967 ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ assurances; Walter Cronkite’s broadcast of 27 February 1968 that the war would ‘end in stalemate’ eroded public support to the point that Johnson, on 31 March 1968, told the country he would not seek re-election. The most useful framing for top-band evaluation is to weigh the tactical victory (Vietcong losses, urban recapture) against the strategic defeat (credibility gap, Cronkite, Johnson’s withdrawal).

Walter Cronkite and the ‘Stalemate’ Broadcast

On the evening of 27 February 1968, after a reporting trip to Vietnam, the CBS Evening News anchor Walter Cronkite closed his programme by telling viewers that the war would ‘end in stalemate’. Cronkite was the most trusted television journalist in the United States; his on-air judgement, made in his own voice rather than as part of a news report, registered as a verdict. President Johnson reportedly told an aide that if he had lost Cronkite, he had lost ‘Mr Average Citizen’. On 31 March Johnson made a televised address: he announced a pause in bombing of most of North Vietnam, opened the door to negotiations, and stated that he would not seek the Democratic nomination for re-election. By June, polls showed that for the first time more Americans called the war a mistake than supported it.

My Lai, March 1968

On the morning of 16 March 1968 American soldiers from Charlie Company, 1st Battalion, 20th Infantry Regiment, entered the South Vietnamese hamlet of My Lai on a search-and-destroy mission. There was no enemy in the hamlet. Over four hours the soldiers killed between 347 and 504 unarmed Vietnamese civilians — mostly women, children and elderly. Some victims were shot in their homes; others were rounded up and machine-gunned in a drainage ditch. Helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson Jr landed his observation aircraft between American troops and a group of fleeing Vietnamese, ordered his crew to fire on his own side if they advanced, and rescued around eleven civilians.

The Army covered up the massacre for over a year. The story broke in the American press in November 1969 in an investigation by the freelance journalist Seymour Hersh, illustrated by the colour photographs that combat photographer Ronald Haeberle had taken on the day. Lieutenant William Calley, the platoon leader, went on trial in November 1970 charged with the premeditated murder of 109 Vietnamese civilians. He was convicted on 29 March 1971 of murdering twenty-two and sentenced to life imprisonment. Within forty-eight hours President Nixon ordered him moved from prison to house arrest at Fort Benning. He was paroled in 1974 after serving around three and a half years.

Key Fact

On 16 March 1968 American soldiers killed between 347 and 504 unarmed Vietnamese civilians at My Lai. The story was broken by Seymour Hersh in November 1969, more than a year after the Army cover-up. Lt William Calley was the only officer convicted of any My Lai-related charge in March 1971; within forty-eight hours President Nixon ordered him moved from prison to house arrest, and he was paroled in 1974.

Kent State, May 1970

On 30 April 1970 President Nixon announced on television that US ground troops had crossed into Cambodia. Anti-war protests, which had thinned during the early withdrawals of the Nixon Doctrine, exploded across more than 350 college campuses in the days that followed. At Kent State University in Ohio the Reserve Officer Training Corps building was set on fire on the evening of 2 May; Governor James Rhodes deployed the Ohio National Guard. On the early afternoon of 4 May 1970 a contingent of around seventy-seven guardsmen, exhausted and inexperienced, opened fire on a crowd of student protesters and bystanders. They fired sixty-seven rounds in around thirteen seconds. The Kent State shootings killed four students — Allison Krause, Jeffrey Miller, Sandra Scheuer and William Schroeder — and wounded nine. Two of the dead were not protesters but students walking between classes.

The killings produced the largest student strike in US history: more than four million students walked out from over 700 campuses, and around 450 universities and colleges shut down for the rest of the spring term. The Pulitzer Prize-winning photograph by John Filo of fourteen-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio kneeling over the body of Jeffrey Miller became the defining image of the home front war.

Hard Hats and the Silent Majority

It would be wrong to think the United States by 1970 was unanimously anti-war. President Nixon had won the 1968 election by appealing to what he would call in a televised address on 3 November 1969 the silent majority: older, mostly white, conservative-leaning Americans who supported the war and disapproved of the protest movement. On 8 May 1970 — four days after Kent State — around two hundred New York construction workers in red, white and blue helmets attacked an anti-war demonstration in lower Manhattan, beating students and breaking up the rally. The hard hats later in the month organised a demonstration of around 100,000 marchers in support of Nixon’s Vietnam policy. The war was now an argument among Americans, on Americans, as much as a war fought against a Vietnamese enemy.

A textbook narrative sometimes presents the United States in 1968-70 as a society sliding uniformly into opposition. The picture was sharper and more divided. The student movement, draft resistance and TV coverage of Tet, My Lai and Kent State did pull middle-American opinion against the war. At the same time Nixon won the 1968 election on a silent-majority appeal, and the hard hats produced visible pro-war counter-protests in 1970. Top-band evaluation answers can use this divide to test interpretations: did the home front turn the war (an anti-war reading), or did it produce a divided politics that Nixon was able to ride for another five years (a silent-majority reading)?
