Within forty-eight hours President Nixon ordered him moved to house arrest at Fort Benning; he was paroled in 1974 after serving around three and a half years.

Shooting on 4 May 1970 in which Ohio National Guardsmen opened fire on student protesters at Kent State University, killing four (Allison Krause, Jeffrey Miller, Sandra Scheuer, William Schroeder) and wounding nine. Triggered by Nixon’s announcement of the Cambodia incursion four days earlier; produced the largest student strike in US history, with more than four million students walking out from over 700 campuses.

Phrase used by President Nixon in a televised address on 3 November 1969 to describe the older, conservative-leaning, mostly white Americans whom he claimed supported his Vietnam policy and disapproved of the anti-war movement; framed the war debate as a contest between a respectable centre and a noisy student fringe.

Construction workers, mostly from New York and other industrial cities, identifiable by their hard hats. Symbolised pro-war working-class Americans; on 8 May 1970 around two hundred attacked an anti-war demonstration in lower Manhattan; later in the month around 100,000 marched in support of Nixon’s Vietnam policy.

practice_questions.text:
Source A: From a private memorandum from Defense Secretary Clark Clifford to President Lyndon B. Johnson, 4 March 1968, after a Pentagon review of the Tet Offensive.

‘The Tet Offensive cannot be read as a military defeat for the United States. Vietcong losses are catastrophic and the urban territory briefly seized has been almost wholly recovered, including Hue. The political effect, however, has been the reverse. The American people had been told the enemy was on the verge of collapse. They have now seen Vietcong soldiers in the grounds of the embassy in Saigon and house-to-house fighting in a city most had never heard of. We must assume that another six months of escalation is not politically available to us.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about the impact of the Tet Offensive.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Senior US officials judged Tet a tactical victory’ supported by ‘Vietcong losses are catastrophic’ or ‘urban territory briefly seized has been almost wholly recovered’ AND ‘Tet had broken the political case for further military escalation’ supported by ‘another six months of escalation is not politically available to us’ or ‘The American people had been told the enemy was on the verge of collapse’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Tet Offensive shifted American public opinion against the Vietnam War in 1968.

You may use the following in your answer:
• Walter Cronkite’s broadcast (27 February 1968)
• the fighting in Hue

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. the credibility gap and Westmoreland’s November 1967 ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ line; the Vietcong commando raid on the US embassy in Saigon; Johnson’s 31 March 1968 withdrawal; the wider role of TV coverage and the draft system) and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. The argument connects the gap between official optimism and televised reality to the changing balance of US public opinion through 1968. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of Tet without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1990 history of the American media in Vietnam):
‘The Tet Offensive was a defeat for the United States because the public believed it was. Walter Cronkite’s broadcast of 27 February 1968 told a country that the war would ‘end in stalemate’, and within five weeks Johnson had withdrawn from the presidential race. Tet was, above all, a media event — a contradiction of the ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ line that the political class could not survive.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2005 study of US military operations in Vietnam):
‘The Tet Offensive was a US-South Vietnamese tactical victory of the first order. Around 40,000 Vietcong fighters died; the southern uprising Hanoi expected did not occur; Hue was recaptured after twenty-five days of urban fighting. The Vietcong were so depleted that the North Vietnamese Army carried the rest of the war. To call Tet a US defeat is to mistake the political reaction in Washington for the military reality in South Vietnam.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about the Tet Offensive? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 sees Tet as a US defeat because of its political and media impact at home, captured by Cronkite’s broadcast and Johnson’s withdrawal; Interpretation 2 sees Tet as a US-South Vietnamese tactical victory in South Vietnam itself, with the ‘defeat’ reading mistaking Washington politics for military reality) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘Tet was, above all, a media event’ vs ‘a US-South Vietnamese tactical victory of the first order’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about the Tet Offensive.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 1990 history of the American media in Vietnam, foregrounding the role of television, Cronkite’s broadcast and the Johnson withdrawal, and so reads Tet through the lens of US public opinion; Interpretation 2 is from a 2005 study of US military operations focused on Vietcong casualties, the recapture of Hue and the depletion of the southern insurgency, and so reads Tet through the lens of the South Vietnamese battlefield. The two have different focuses (US politics and media vs South Vietnamese military outcomes) and use different bodies of evidence (US press archives and the Cronkite broadcast vs operational reports from Vietnam), and so reach different verdicts on whether Tet was a US defeat.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about the Tet Offensive?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across 1967-68 (Westmoreland’s November 1967 ‘light at the end of the tunnel’ line; the Tet Offensive of 30 January 1968 and the more than 100 attacks; the Vietcong raid on the US embassy in Saigon; the twenty-five-day battle for Hue and around 40,000 Vietcong dead; the credibility gap; Cronkite’s 27 February broadcast; Johnson’s 31 March withdrawal; later wider home-front events such as My Lai, the Calley trial, Kent State and the silent majority that show how divided the political fallout actually was), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1. [16 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: From a 1971 letter from a Kent State University professor to a colleague at another Ohio campus, written shortly after the 4 May 1970 shootings.

‘The killings here have changed how the country argues about Vietnam. Within hours of Mr Filo’s photograph reaching the wires we had calls from professors in California and Texas asking how to keep their own campuses calm. By the end of that week the universities had effectively closed for the term. The President describes the protesters as bums; New York construction workers attacked our students in lower Manhattan; my own colleagues are split between those who believe the country has had enough of the war and those who believe it has had enough of student protest.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about the impact of the Kent State shootings on the United States.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘Kent State produced a national wave of campus protest and shutdowns’ supported by ‘By the end of that week the universities had effectively closed for the term’ AND ‘Kent State did not unite the country against the war but deepened a divide between anti-war and pro-war Americans’ supported by ‘my own colleagues are split between those who believe the country has had enough of the war and those who believe it has had enough of student protest’ or ‘New York construction workers attacked our students’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

lessons.title: Vietnamisation, Paris and Why the US Lost, 1969-75

practice_questions.text:
Source A: From an internal memorandum from Henry Kissinger to President Nixon, 10 September 1971, on the prospects for the Paris peace talks.

‘Hanoi’s position has hardened since Lam Son 719. The North Vietnamese have concluded that the South Vietnamese army cannot hold the country alone and that the United States will not stay. We must therefore exit on terms that protect the appearance of an honourable settlement and that buy a sufficient interval before the inevitable test of South Vietnam’s independent capacity. The bombing of the North, if necessary on a far heavier scale than yet attempted, may be the lever required to bring Le Duc Tho back to the table.’

Give two things you can infer from Source A about US thinking on the peace talks in 1971.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct inferences each supported by a quoted detail (e.g. ‘US officials privately doubted that South Vietnam could survive on its own once US forces left’ supported by ‘the South Vietnamese army cannot hold the country alone’ or ‘a sufficient interval before the inevitable test’ AND ‘Kissinger saw the bombing of North Vietnam as a tool to force concessions in Paris rather than to win the war’ supported by ‘the bombing of the North … may be the lever required to bring Le Duc Tho back to the table’.)
Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Vietnamisation failed to secure South Vietnam between 1969 and 1975.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Cambodia incursion (1970)
• the fall of Saigon (1975)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained causal argument that uses both stimulus points AND introduces a third own-knowledge factor (e.g. the political weakness of South Vietnam, ARVN corruption and the failure of Lam Son 719, the impact of Watergate and congressional aid cuts in 1974-75, the terms of the Paris Peace Agreement that left around 150,000 North Vietnamese troops inside South Vietnam) and reaches a substantiated judgement on relative importance. The argument connects withdrawal of US troops from over 540,000 in 1969 to around 24,000 by the end of 1972 with the structural weaknesses of the South Vietnamese state. Uses precise period terminology consistently.
Secure: Clear causal explanation covering both stimulus points plus a third factor; judgement offered though less fully substantiated.
Developing: Some analysis of stimulus points; the third factor is asserted rather than developed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of Vietnamisation without explicit causal explanation, or stimulus-only with no third factor. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Interpretation 1 (from a 1985 study of the Vietnam War):
‘The United States lost the war in Vietnam mainly because of the strength of the enemy. The Vietcong’s guerrilla tactics, the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia, integration with the peasant population and Russian and Chinese material support gave Hanoi a strategic depth no Western army could counter. The fall of Saigon in 1975 was the consequence of an enemy whose patience and political capacity always exceeded America’s.’

Interpretation 2 (from a 2010 study of US strategy in Indochina):
‘The United States lost the war in Vietnam mainly because of its own strategic and political failures. The body-count tactics of search and destroy, the bombing campaigns that radicalised the home front, the political collapse of South Vietnam under an army with no rural legitimacy, the credibility gap after Tet 1968, and the congressional aid cuts after Watergate all turned American power against itself. The Vietcong did not defeat the United States; the United States defeated itself.’

How does Interpretation 1 differ from Interpretation 2 about why the United States lost the Vietnam War? Explain your answer using Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a substantive disagreement (Interpretation 1 explains American defeat as the consequence of North Vietnamese and Vietcong strength — guerrilla tactics, the Trail, peasant integration, Russian and Chinese support; Interpretation 2 explains American defeat as the consequence of US strategic and political failures — search and destroy, bombing, the credibility gap, the political weakness of South Vietnam, congressional aid cuts) AND quotes a precise phrase from each interpretation as evidence (e.g. ‘the consequence of an enemy whose patience and political capacity always exceeded America’s’ vs ‘the United States defeated itself’).
Secure: A clear difference identified with quotations from both interpretations.
Developing: Lists factual content of each interpretation without showing the contrast.
Emerging: Paraphrases without identifying disagreement. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 give different views about why the United States lost the Vietnam War.

You may use Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2 to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed reason linked specifically to the two interpretations. For example: Interpretation 1 is from a 1985 study of the Vietnam War, written when Cold War framing dominated and when Vietcong and North Vietnamese strengths were the natural focus, drawing on military operations and supply-line evidence; Interpretation 2 is from a 2010 study of US strategy in Indochina, written after the opening of the Pentagon archives and the Watergate-era papers, drawing on US presidential records and so foregrounding the failures of search and destroy, the credibility gap, ARVN weakness and the impact of Watergate. The two have different focuses (enemy strength vs US strategic and political failure) and use different bodies of evidence (Vietcong operations vs US strategy archives), and so reach different verdicts on why the United States lost.
Secure: A plausible reason linked to authors’ purpose, evidence used or focus, with reference to both extracts.
Developing: A general reason (‘they used different sources’) without anchoring to either extract.
Emerging: A vague claim about ‘bias’ or ‘different point of view’. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 1 about why the United States lost the Vietnam War?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.

In your answer you should:
• give arguments for and against Interpretation 1
• use both interpretations and your own knowledge of the historical context
• reach a substantiated judgement

Marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar will be awarded for this answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates BOTH interpretations explicitly, deploys substantial own knowledge across 1969-75 (Vietnamisation and US troop withdrawal from over 540,000 to around 24,000; the Nixon Doctrine of July 1969; ARVN corruption and the failure of Operation Lam Son 719 in 1971; the Cambodia incursion of 1970 and Kent State; Operation Linebacker II of December 1972; the Paris Peace Agreement of 27 January 1973 and the around 150,000 North Vietnamese troops left inside the South; the Vietcong’s guerrilla tactics and the Ho Chi Minh Trail; Russian and Chinese support; congressional aid cuts after Watergate in 1974-75; the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975), and reaches a substantiated judgement on Interpretation 1. Uses precise period terminology consistently and writes with sustained accuracy in spelling, punctuation and grammar (full SPaG band).
Secure: Both interpretations addressed and supported with relevant own knowledge; a judgement offered but less fully substantiated; SPaG generally accurate.
Developing: One interpretation evaluated more fully than the other; own knowledge partial; judgement implicit; SPaG inconsistent.
Emerging: A knowledge essay only loosely linked to either interpretation; no clear judgement on Interpretation 1; SPaG limits clarity. [20 marks — 16 content + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Source B: From a 1975 retrospective interview with a former South Vietnamese army officer recorded for a US oral history project shortly after the fall of Saigon.

‘The Americans gave us helicopters, M16 rifles and tanks. They could not give us a country. After 1973 they were gone, and in 1974 the Congress in Washington cut the money. Our generals were political appointees; many of them ran when the offensive came in March 1975. The peasants in the highlands had no reason to fight for Saigon. We were left with everything except the only thing that mattered — a state the people would defend.’

Give two things you can infer from Source B about why South Vietnam fell in 1975.

Secure: Two valid inferences with at least one supporting quotation.
Developing: One inference with quotation; a second point that paraphrases.
Emerging: Summary of the source. [4 marks — 2 marks per inference: 1 for inference, 1 for quotation]
